tier_reason: benchmarks/README.md carries every number in the record and the raw Google Benchmark JSON under benchmarks/results/ matches it (e.g. 5M clean materialize median 739.6 ms vs 2,104.5 ms); the harness is public (benchmarks/csv_parser_multi_pass_bench.cpp vs benchmarks/fast_cpp_csv_parser_multi_pass_bench.cpp, csv_parser_fast_cpp_read_bench.cpp, glaze_csv_*_bench.cpp, dataframe_rapidcsv_roundtrip_bench.cpp, built by benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler MSVC 19.50, flags recoverable from public CMake files (Release plus /arch:AVX2 as a PUBLIC option of the csv target) and CPU i5-12400 are stated, so A holds.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, C++20 (Glaze targets C++23), CMake Release configuration (MSVC Release defaults; benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt adds no optimization flags), /arch:AVX2 added as a PUBLIC compile option of the csv library target in include/internal/CMakeLists.txt (so it reaches every benchmark binary that links csv, but not the standalone fast_cpp_csv_parser_* and glaze_csv_* binaries), CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark v1.8.5 via FetchContent; fast-cpp-csv-parser and rapidcsv fetched at unpinned master, Glaze v7.5.0
corrections.claimed_speedup: Median real time, generated 8-column CSV. One-pass materialization (single parser worker) vs fast-cpp-csv-parser: 5M clean 739.6 ms vs 2,105 ms (2.8x, derived from page data), 5M quoted 930.6 ms vs 2,489 ms (2.7x, derived from page data), 500K clean 156.8 ms vs 218.8 ms (1.4x, derived from page data). Materialize plus multi-pass aggregation (the README's 'closest apples-to-apples' table): 5M clean 1,251 ms vs 2,252 ms (1.8x, derived from page data), 5M quoted 1,517 ms vs 3,090 ms (2.0x, derived from page data), but only 215.4 vs 237.1 ms and 262.9 vs 280.7 ms at 500K (about 1.1x, derived from page data). Positional read with 4 speculative parser workers overtakes fast-cpp-csv-parser (5M clean 702.2 ms vs 915.1 ms; spec-8 605.0 ms). Versus rapidcsv: DataFrame load 1.48x (500K multiline, 220.4 vs 325.2 ms, derived from page data) to 4.53x (5M multiline) faster, load+save 2.17x to 3.58x faster. Versus Glaze CSV reader: 5M clean materialization 739.6 ms vs 1,972 ms. It loses the small raw reads (500K clean count 146.5 ms vs 81.8 ms, read 164.9 ms vs 82.8 ms for fast-cpp-csv-parser) and the multi-pass-only step on already materialized rows (5M clean 479.5 ms vs 141.6 ms for fast-cpp-csv-parser, from benchmarks/results/5000000_rows/clean/*_multi_pass_bench.json).
corrections.caveats: Project's own benchmarks, one machine, one OS and one compiler (Windows 11, MSVC 19.50), result JSON dated 2026-05-08 while the library has changed since (last commit 2026-10-06), so ordering may shift on GCC/Clang, Linux or newer code. The 'materialization' tables compare different amounts of work: csv-parser pushes CSVRow handles that keep parser-owned buffers alive and parse fields lazily on get<>, while fast-cpp-csv-parser copies six std::string fields and converts two integers per row into a struct (and Glaze deserializes into reflected structs); the cost shows up later, where csv-parser's multi-pass step on materialized rows is 3.4x slower (479.5 ms vs 141.6 ms at 5M clean). The fairer materialize+aggregation table still favours csv-parser, by about 1.1x at 500K rows and 1.8-2.0x at 5M rows. Flag asymmetry: /arch:AVX2 is a PUBLIC option of the csv target, so csv-parser binaries (and both libraries inside csv_parser_fast_cpp_read_bench) build with AVX2 while the standalone fast_cpp_csv_parser_* and glaze_csv_* binaries build with the MSVC default ISA. fast-cpp-csv-parser wins the 500K raw read and count tests; csv-parser times grow sublinearly from 500K to 5M rows (count 146.5 to 547.6 ms), so fixed start-up cost dominates the small runs. The rapidcsv comparison pits csv-parser's filename path (memory-mapped reader with its background worker thread on, CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON) against rapidcsv's single-threaded Document. Comparison libraries are fetched at unpinned master (fast-cpp-csv-parser, rapidcsv). No comparison against std::getline or any libstdc++/libc++ code was found. 'Likely one of the fastest general-purpose C++ CSV ETL libraries' is the author's wording. Inputs are generated, not real-world data (the README's Kaggle-file timings, such as 1.4 GB in about 0.5 s on warm cache, have no baseline).

notes: Numbers match the README and the tracked result JSON; tier A stands (public harness, MSVC 19.50, Release plus /arch:AVX2 from public CMake files, i5-12400). Record shortcomings: materialization tables compare lazy CSVRow handles with fast-cpp's eager std::string structs (csv-parser then loses the multi-pass-only step 479.5 vs 141.6 ms), AVX2 only on the csv-parser binaries, Windows/MSVC single machine, results from 2026-05-08 code. baseline_in_list set true because the category's baselines are 'csv-parser libs the benchmark names'; metadata (MIT, 1.1k stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-06) verified on github.com.

tier_reason: The only numbers reachable are an OpenWrt packager's commit message (Snort 3.1.84.0 through a router with and without Vectorscan 5.4.11, n=3 per cell, speedtest download rate): third-party but with no benchmark code, compiler, flags or CPU model, and no well-known suite or paper, so C. The Arm blog claim of a 20-40% Snort uplift on Ampere Altra (snippet only) comes from a co-developer of Vectorscan and is also C.

corrections.baseline: Snort 3 built without Vectorscan (the OpenWrt snort3 package sets -DENABLE_HYPERSCAN only when the vectorscan package is selected, so Snort falls back to its built-in non-Hyperscan fast-pattern search methods and PCRE; the commit message does not name the search_method used)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snort 3.1.84.0 download throughput through the router, with vs without Vectorscan 5.4.11, n=3: GL.iNet GL-MT6000 (flogic, kernel 6.6.26) IDS mode 331.0 +/-27.34 vs 91.2 +/-0.21 Mbit/s (3.6x), IPS mode 52.9 +/-0.78 vs 30.0 +/-0.06 Mbit/s (1.8x); Raspberry Pi 5B (bcm2712, kernel 6.1.86) IPS mode 232.8 +/-0.26 vs 164.3 +/-0.64 Mbit/s (1.4x). The commit notes single-core CPU saturation in all runs. Snippet only, not opened: Arm's blog reports a 20-40% uplift over Snort's default regex implementations on a Neoverse N1 (Ampere Altra); Wordfence's CLI 4.0.1 post reports 6x to 30x faster malware scans with Vectorscan or Hyperscan instead of PCRE.
corrections.caveats: The only numeric comparison reachable is a packager's commit message in the OpenWrt packages repository (third party, not the project's own repo). It measures Snort 3 as a whole through a router with a speedtest script against a roughly 22 MB community ruleset, not the regex engine in isolation, and the baseline is 'Snort without Vectorscan' with the fallback matcher unnamed, so the speedups are whole-application gains and mostly reflect the Hyperscan design that Vectorscan inherits rather than Vectorscan-specific work. Compiler, flags and exact CPU models are not stated, no benchmark code is public, n=3 per cell. The README links a wiki 'Vectorscan Benchmarks' page that does not exist (the wiki index lists only Home and two installation pages). benchmarks/benchmarks.cpp is an internal microbenchmark of its own primitives (shufti, truffle, noodle and so on) with no baseline. The Arm Neoverse blog (20-40% Snort uplift on Ampere Altra) and Wordfence CLI post (6x-30x vs PCRE, Vectorscan or Hyperscan) were blocked by the egress policy and are snippet only; Arm co-develops Vectorscan, so its figure is first-party. Later correctness fixes postdate the measured 5.4.11: an arm64 HS_FLAG_DOTALL false-negative bug (issue #382, reported on 5.4.12, regression tests in #391), SVE accelerator bugs in shufti/truffle/noodle (#377), a NEON rshift fallback bug (#396) and a stack buffer overflow in rvermicelliDoubleExecReal (#392) were fixed for 5.4.13; whether 5.4.11 on these ARM boards was affected is not established. The patch's author date reads May 2023 while the message cites Snort 3.1.84.0 and Vectorscan 5.4.11, so the numbers were evidently added when the long-running PR was revised. No comparison against std::regex, RE2, PCRE2 or Hyperscan itself was found.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 766 stars, 93 forks; packaged in OpenWrt (with Snort 3) and in Debian-family and other distributions as libvectorscan

notes: Numbers in the record match the OpenWrt commit (d62471c, libs/vectorscan/Makefile, PKG_VERSION 5.4.11); tier C stands; metadata verified on github.com (BSD-3-Clause, 766 stars, GitHub-marked fork of intel/hyperscan, default branch develop, last commit 2026-09-04, release 5.4.13 on 2026-08-21). Fork judgement: keep as a separate entry, not a duplicate of the listed Hyperscan, because it changes performance-relevant code (SIMD layer rewritten as SuperVector templates with NEON/ASIMD, SVE/SVE2 and VSX backends), its own evidence is on ARM boards where Hyperscan cannot run, and it is the maintained BSD line now that Hyperscan 5.5+ is closed source; record as a shortcoming that the measured gain is whole-Snort vs an unnamed fallback matcher and mostly reflects inherited Hyperscan algorithms. Wiki Benchmarks link is dead; later arm64 correctness fixes postdate the measured 5.4.11.
